summary: Chaim of Volozhin (1749-1821) was the foremost disciple of Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, the Vilna Gaon, and the founder in 1802 of the Volozhin Yeshiva, the institution regarded as the prototype of the modern Lithuanian yeshiva. He is the author of Nefesh ha-Chayim ('The Soul of Life'), the systematic theological statement of the Mitnagdic worldview, which sets out the supremacy of Torah study, undertaken for its own sake (lishmah), as the highest form of divine service. This entry records his roles as the Gaon's disciple, the founder of Volozhin, and the theologian of the Lithuanian tradition, with the ideal of study attributed to him and to that tradition.
description:
Chaim ben Isaac of Volozhin (Valozhyn), born in 1749 and active in the Lithuanian lands within the Russian Empire, is recorded in the tradition as the foremost disciple of Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, the Vilna Gaon (ha-Gra), the towering figure of Lithuanian rabbinic learning and the leading opponent of the nascent Hasidic movement. Chaim studied with the Gaon and became, in the accounts, the principal transmitter and institutional heir of his master's approach to Torah study, and he died in 1821.

In 1802 (traditionally 1802/1803) Chaim founded the yeshiva of Volozhin, formally Yeshivat Etz Chaim ('Tree of Life'), which the scholarship, chiefly that of Shaul Stampfer, treats as the prototype of the modern Lithuanian yeshiva: an independent institution of full-time advanced Talmud study, supported by contributions gathered from a wide public rather than by the local community, and drawing students from afar, distinct from the older pattern of study organized within the local town. Volozhin became the 'mother of the yeshivas', the model for the network of Lithuanian yeshivas that followed through the nineteenth century, and its structure shaped much of the modern yeshiva world (the volozhin-yeshiva entry treats the institution in detail).

Chaim's theological work is the Nefesh ha-Chayim ('The Soul of Life'), published after his death, which is read in the tradition and in scholarship as the systematic statement of the Mitnagdic (Lithuanian, non-Hasidic) worldview, in particular of the supremacy of Torah study. In the fourth gate of that work, whose opening chapter is open and auditable on Sefaria and was read directly, Chaim sets out the tremendous obligation of the involvement with Torah (esek ha-Torah) incumbent on every person of Israel day and night, and holds that the direct, steady study of the Torah itself, the written and the oral, undertaken for its own sake (lishmah) and joined to the awe or fear of God, is the highest religious occupation. He warns there, in the read passage, against those who, though their intention is for Heaven, make the core of their study the books of ethical and devotional instruction (sifrei yirah u-musar) rather than the direct study of scripture and the myriad laws, teaching that this 'is not the path' in which the light of the Torah rests. This valuation of study is given here as the attributed ideal of Chaim and of the Lithuanian (Mitnagdic) tradition, described and not affirmed or denied by the editor.

The Nefesh ha-Chayim is also read as articulating, on the Mitnagdic side, a theology of the divine presence and of the human role in sustaining the worlds through Torah and mitzvot, developed in the accounts partly in engagement with the emphases of the contemporaneous Hasidic movement; the wider dispute between the Mitnagdim, the Lithuanian circles of the Vilna Gaon, and the Hasidim stands in the background of Chaim's life and work, and it is noted here as historical context and treated elsewhere in the dataset as a dispute with both sides attributed and not adjudicated. This entry presents Chaim of Volozhin on the tradition's own terms as the Gaon's disciple, the founder of Volozhin, and the theologian of the Mitnagdic ideal of study, with the scholarship recorded alongside as attributed sources.

NEUTRALITY: the ideal of the supremacy of Torah study, undertaken lishmah and joined to awe of God as the highest divine service, and the theology of the divine presence developed in Nefesh ha-Chayim, are stated as the ATTRIBUTED ideal and teaching of Chaim and of the Lithuanian/Mitnagdic tradition ('given here as the attributed ideal... described and not affirmed or denied by the editor'), not endorsed.
